text:
Sustainable aviation fuel (SAF) and renewable diesel (RD) project developer Jet Zero Australia announced today that it has raised $30 million in a new funding round, with proceeds from the financing aimed at advancing the company’s Project Ulysses, a commercial-scale SAF and RD refinery in Townsville, Australia.

Founded in 2021 North Queensland by Ed Mason, Jet Zero develops and operates sustainable aviation fuel (SAF) and renewable diesel projects, focusing on developing a biofuels production capacity in regional Australia.

The company said that the new capital will primarily fund completion of Front-End Engineering Design and support the project’s continued advancement towards Final Investment Decision and construction.

The funding round received backing from institutional investors including Qantas and Airbus, both of which had initially invested in Jet Zero in 2023. Jet Zero also announced that South Korean global trading and energy company Posco International will join the company as a strategic investor, with the companies exploring opportunities across fuel offtake, infrastructure and feedstock, subject to further agreement.

Ed Mason, Jet Zero Australia Chief Executive Officer, said:

“Completing our $30 million funding round, welcoming POSCO INTERNATIONAL and securing final development approval are defining milestones for Project Ulysses… Some organisations will buy low carbon liquid fuels. Others will invest in building the industry. We are fortunate to be backed by organisations committed to doing both.”

Jet Zero said that the new project has received its final Development Permit Decision Notice from the Queensland Office of the Coordinator-General, completing its principal development approvals.

According to the company, the project is expected to create approximately 1,000 jobs during construction and 100 permanent operational roles, while supporting the development of a broader Australian biofuels industry capable of supporting more than 18,000 jobs by 2040 across feedstock production, agriculture, refining, manufacturing and logistics.

Fiona Messent, Qantas Group Chief Sustainability Officer, said:

“Establishing domestic SAF production in Australia will support fuel security, create jobs and help aviation and Australia meet its decarbonisation objectives. Australia has the feedstock and the industry support to refine SAF here, and companies like Jet Zero can help put that to work.”

text:
Cathay Pacific and Google trial AI technology to cut climate impact of aircraft trails

Google and Cathay Pacific have partnered to test AI-powered technology that could help airlines avoid conditions that lead to persistent aircraft contrails, which can contribute to atmospheric warming. The trial is being conducted across Cathay Pacific's flight network, with a second phase now planned to collect more operational data. Cathay Pacific is Google's first commercial airline partner in Asia-Pacific to trial the contrail mitigation technology and the first airline globally to test the system on ultra-long-haul flights.

How the AI system identifies contrail-forming areas

Google's system combines AI-based predictive models, satellite imagery and weather data to forecast areas where aircraft are likely to form contrails. Flight dispatchers and pilots can use the forecasts to adjust an aircraft's altitude and route to avoid those areas. Cathay Pacific integrates the forecasts into its Electronic Flight Folder, alongside real-time operational information, allowing pilots to access the data in the cockpit.

What are aircraft contrails

Contrails are thin clouds that can form behind aircraft when they fly through cold and humid conditions at high altitude. While many disappear quickly, some can persist and spread into larger cloud formations that trap heat in the atmosphere. The companies cited previous research suggesting that persistent contrails could account for around one-third of aviation's total climate impact, making them an area of research alongside carbon dioxide emissions.

Trial covered more than 100 flights

The initial operational trial began in late 2025 and targeted more than 100 flights across Cathay Pacific's network. More than 80 flights ultimately followed contrail-avoidance routes. Google estimates that those flights achieved about a 40% reduction in the warming impact of contrails. The release notes that not all of the targeted flights participated because of factors including airspace and payload restrictions. The Hong Kong-Singapore corridor was among the routes tested. Early analysis found that relatively small altitude adjustments could prevent contrail formation, with actions on that route accounting for more than half of the trial's total climate impact.

Second phase will expand flight trials

Google and Cathay Pacific are now starting a larger second phase of trials across Cathay's Asia and transpacific network. The partners said the additional flights will provide more real-world operational data to assess contrail avoidance and its potential climate benefits. Nonprofit initiative Contrails.org is also participating in the project. The companies said more research is needed to determine how contrail avoidance could work across different airlines and airspaces. The resulting data could also contribute to future industry practices and policy discussions.

Cathay Pacific continues to focus on carbon dioxide emissions

Cathay Pacific said reducing carbon dioxide emissions remains a primary focus through measures including fleet modernisation, operational efficiency improvements and the use of sustainable aviation fuel. The partnership with Google is focused on the separate issue of non-CO₂ climate effects, including contrails.

text:
James Tam, Co-Chairman of EcoCeres, the global renewable energy firm, explores how best to scale SAF during increasingly unstable times

As 2026 unfolds in an age of geopolitical fragmentation, the debate over sustainable aviation is changing. The central question is no longer just how fast we can decarbonise, but whether the world can produce enough sustainable aviation fuel (SAF) at a pace, quality, and scale that can withstand a highly unstable operating environment.

In a period of disrupted supply chains and renewed geopolitical tension, aviation needs fuel systems that are not only lower in carbon, but also more secure and resilient. The next phase of decarbonisation will be decided by whether SAF can be produced and delivered at scale, under credible standards, in the places that need it most.

From pledges to dependable supply

For sustainable aviation, the bottleneck is not a lack of commitment; it is turning those commitments into dependable supply. SAF projects must remain viable through fuel-price swings, policy cycles, and geopolitical shocks. That requires more than technology (although that has been highlighted as a major bottleneck by IATA); it demands durable policy support, diversified feedstock strategies, and regional value chains that can perform under pressure.

While SAF is already used commercially, projected global output still represents only a small fraction of jet fuel demand. The distance between climate goals and available supply is now impossible to ignore. For regulators and producers, the challenge is how to create demand certainty and clear standards, while leaving enough flexibility for technologies and feedstocks to evolve.

Why diversification matters now

Diversification must sit at the centre of SAF strategy. Today a large share of production comes from pathways using waste oils and fats. These routes have been essential in getting the market started, but they cannot on their own deliver the scale required for global aviation in the coming decades.

The sector will need a broader portfolio of feedstocks and technologies, including agricultural residues, forestry residues, municipal solid waste, alcohol-to-jet pathways and, over time, e-SAF or other emerging power-to-liquid options. A diversified system is more secure, more scalable, and significantly less vulnerable to disruption than one dependent on a narrow pool of globally traded feedstocks.

Read more: How methanol-to-jet can help scale SAF

Read more: Weakening HEFA cap risks green hydrogen e-SAF demand

Energy security in a fractured world

Recent global events have underscored how exposed aviation remains to traditional fossil-fuel supply chains. During recent geopolitical conflicts, the International Energy Agency warned of rapidly dwindling jet fuel reserves in Europe as flows through critical chokepoints such as the Strait of Hormuz were constrained. Airlines cut flights to save fuel, and nations drew down strategic petroleum reserves at unprecedented rates just to keep their economies moving.

These episodes highlight two structural vulnerabilities in how the world powers aviation today. First, jet fuel remains overwhelmingly derived from crude oil, tieing airlines directly to the geopolitics of oil markets. Second, the system relies heavily on long-haul sea routes to move fuel from a limited number of production centres to demand hubs around the world.

SAF offers a direct way to ease both pressure points. By replacing a significant share of fossil-based jet fuel with waste- and residue-based SAF, the industry can gradually reduce its direct exposure to crude oil markets. And when SAF is produced from local feedstocks and then refined, blended and uplifted close to the airports where it is used, it reduces dependence on vulnerable long-distance sea routes.

Expert view: Why combining biomass and green hydrogen may solve SAF’s scaling problem

A “local to local” test bed

This “local to local” model is particularly relevant for Asia’s major aviation hubs. The Guangdong–Hong Kong–Macao Greater Bay Area is moving from concept to practice, offering a blueprint for how an aviation hub can cut emissions and strengthen energy resilience at the same time. Few regions combine such a dense aviation network, manufacturing base, logistics capability and access to waste-based feedstocks within one integrated economic geography.

The broader lesson is that sustainable aviation will not scale on climate ambition alone. It will scale when SAF systems are designed to be credible, diversified, and resilient, and when regions build value chains that reflect local strengths rather than copying a single global template.

Waste-to-fuel pathways now emerging in the Greater Bay Area, including those being advanced by EcoCeres, offer one example of how this can be achieved. By turning local waste streams into strategic low-carbon fuel supply, these models point towards a more robust future for aviation — one that is lower in emissions, more secure in energy, and far more resilient to global shocks.

text:
Cathay Pacific and Google today announced a partnership to advance research on contrails and their contribution to aviation’s climate impact. Cathay Pacific is Google’s first commercial airline partner in Asia-Pacific to trial its AI-powered contrail mitigation technology, and the first airline globally to test contrail avoidance on ultra-long-haul flights. The companies have started trials to evaluate the operational feasibility and constraints of contrail avoidance across Cathay Pacific’s extensive global network. The trials will contribute valuable new data to global contrail research and advance understanding of contrail formation and avoidance in the Asia-Pacific region, a geography that has been underrepresented in previous trials. The real-world data gathered through the trial would allow the industry to better understand the climate benefits of contrail avoidance in actual operational environments.

The thin white lines that sometimes form behind aircraft in the sky are known as contrails, or condensation trails. They are clouds that form when aircrafts fly through certain cold and humid conditions at high altitude. While many disappear quickly, some persist and spread into broader cloud formations that can trap heat in the atmosphere. Previous research suggests these persistent contrails could account for around one-third of aviation's total climate impact, making them an important area of study alongside carbon dioxide (CO₂) emissions.

Cathay recognises aviation’s contribution to climate change and is working towards addressing the climate impacts through multiple approaches. Reducing CO₂ emissions remains a primary focus for Cathay through fleet modernisation, operational efficiency improvements and the adoption of sustainable aviation fuel (SAF). At the same time, the airline recognises the importance of growing scientific understanding of non-CO₂ climate effects, including contrails. Through this partnership, Cathay Pacific and Google are supporting contrail research using real-world operational data from flight trials. The insights will help build further understanding of the impact and possible actions airlines can take against individual contrails, while exploring how contrail avoidance could be implemented and managed at scale across the aviation industry.

AI in the Cockpit Shows Encouraging Early Results

Google’s contrail mitigation solution combines AI-based predictive models, satellite imagery detection tools, and extensive weather intelligence to forecast contrail-forming zones. This actionable data allows flight dispatchers and pilots to make informed altitude adjustments navigating around these zones much like they routinely do to avoid turbulence.

Onboard, Cathay Pacific leverages its modernised fleet capabilities, combining in-flight Wi-Fi connectivity with its proprietary, in-house developed Electronic Flight Folder (EFF). The EFF system equips pilots with dynamic Google contrail forecasts alongside real-time operational parameters, enabling seamless decision-making in the cockpit without disrupting normal operations.

An operational trial began in late 2025, with more than 100 flights targeted across Cathay Pacific's network. Over 80 flights followed contrail-avoidance routes, and Google estimates that these flights achieved roughly 40% reduction in the warming impact of contrails.

The Hong Kong-Singapore corridor was one of the routes tested, as flights in this airspace frequently encounter conditions where persistent contrails form. Early analysis indicates that minor altitude adjustments can successfully prevent contrails, with actions taken on this single route accounting for more than 50% of the trial's total climate impact.

Lawrence Fong, Director Digital and IT, Cathay said: “Aviation needs solutions to address climate change, and AI is accelerating that progress. This partnership combines Cathay’s operational expertise with Google’s world-class AI capabilities to tackle complex sustainability challenges at scale. At Cathay, we believe innovation should deliver tangible and meaningful impact, and this collaboration sets a new benchmark for leadership in our industry."

Michael Yue, Managing Director and General Manager, Google Hong Kong said: “At Google, we believe AI has the power to help address complex environmental challenges and our partnership with Cathay Pacific is a prime example of this in action—researching how predictive AI can be deployed in live operations to help address the climate impact of contrails with today’s aircrafts and today’s fuel. This work reflects our ongoing commitment to developing sustainable solutions that deliver lasting impact, and we’re excited to expand our trial with Cathay Pacific and continue contributing to open climate science together.”

Shaping the Future of Aviation

The initial trial provided valuable experience for integrating predictive AI data in live flight planning to support contrail avoidance at flights level, while bringing together the operational and technical stakeholders needed to make such trials possible. While the partnership delivered encouraging results on individual flights, further trials and research are needed to assess the benefits of applying contrail avoidance measures across airlines and airspaces. The availability of such robust science evidence will enable further industry considerations and policy development by airlines, regulators, and other industry players.

Therefore, the partners are embarking on a larger second phase of flight trials to generate a broader set of real-world operational data and further insights across Cathay Pacific’s Asia and transpacific network. Contrails.org, a nonprofit initiative dedicated to advancing the science of contrail mitigation, is also a partner in the project. The ongoing partnership aims to generate a robust operational data set to further scientific understanding of contrail avoidance and help inform future industry best practices.

Contrails are the thin white trails often seen behind aircraft flying at high altitudes. These trails are created when hot aircraft engine emissions mix with cold, humid air, causing water vapour to freeze into tiny ice crystals that form cloud-like streaks.

The operational testing programme began in late 2025, with more than 100 Cathay Pacific flights selected for evaluation across the airline’s global network.

More than 80 flights operated using routes designed to reduce contrail formation. According to Google’s early assessment, these flights achieved an estimated 40% reduction in the warming effect linked to contrails.

One of the key trial routes was the Hong Kong–Singapore corridor, where atmospheric conditions frequently support persistent contrail formation. Initial findings showed that relatively small altitude adjustments could prevent contrails from developing under suitable conditions.

The Hong Kong–Singapore route produced particularly notable results, contributing more than half of the total climate benefit recorded during the trial period.

New Data Could Shape the Future of Sustainable Aviation

The partnership between Cathay Pacific and Google highlights the growing role of artificial intelligence in addressing aviation’s environmental challenges. While reducing carbon emissions remains a central priority for airlines worldwide, researchers are increasingly examining non-CO₂ factors that influence aviation’s climate impact.

The information collected through these trials will help improve scientific understanding of contrail behaviour and provide airlines with practical knowledge about implementing avoidance strategies on a wider scale.

As global aviation continues to grow, technologies that support more efficient and climate-conscious operations are expected to become increasingly important. The Cathay Pacific and Google initiative represents one of the latest efforts to combine aviation expertise, artificial intelligence and atmospheric research to create a more sustainable future for air travel.

Lawrence Fong, Director Digital and IT, Cathay said: “Aviation needs solutions to address climate change, and AI is accelerating that progress. This partnership combines Cathay’s operational expertise with Google’s world-class AI capabilities to tackle complex sustainability challenges at scale. At Cathay, we believe innovation should deliver tangible and meaningful impact, and this collaboration sets a new benchmark for leadership in our industry.”

Michael Yue, Managing Director and General Manager, Google Hong Kong said: “At Google, we believe AI has the power to help address complex environmental challenges and our partnership with Cathay Pacific is a prime example of this in action—researching how predictive AI can be deployed in live operations to help address the climate impact of contrails with today’s aircrafts and today’s fuel. This work reflects our ongoing commitment to developing sustainable solutions that deliver lasting impact, and we’re excited to expand our trial with Cathay Pacific and continue contributing to open climate science together.”

Shaping the Next Era of Sustainable Aviation

The first phase of the trial delivered important insights into how predictive artificial intelligence data can be integrated into real-time flight planning to support contrail avoidance at the individual flight level. The initiative also helped bring together key operational and technical partners required to conduct such advanced aviation trials.

Although the collaboration produced promising outcomes on selected flights, additional research and expanded testing are required to understand the wider impact of implementing contrail avoidance strategies across broader airline networks and airspace systems. Strong scientific evidence from these studies will support future decisions by airlines, aviation authorities, regulators and other industry stakeholders as they evaluate potential policies and operational standards.

Building on the early findings, the partners are now moving into a larger second phase of flight trials. This next stage will collect a wider range of real-world operational data and provide deeper insights from flights across Cathay Pacific’s regional Asia network and transpacific routes.

The project also includes collaboration with Contrails.org, a non-profit organisation focused on advancing scientific research and solutions related to contrail mitigation. Through continued cooperation, the partners aim to develop a comprehensive operational dataset that can strengthen global understanding of contrail avoidance, support future aviation research and contribute to the development of industry best practices.

text:
Andrew Clarke, senior engineer-design & analysis and Becky Petry, engineer III-design & analysis, Greene Tweed explain how advanced elastomer seals enable scalable SAF adoption in aerospace.

Sustainable aviation fuel (SAF), sometimes referred to as SATF (Synthetic Aviation Turbine Fuel), is increasingly viewed as one of the most practical near-term pathways for reducing aviation emissions. This is because it can be directly introduced within existing aircraft fleets, airport infrastructure and fuelling networks. However, while SAF offers significant sustainability benefits, its unique chemistry presents new challenges for aircraft fuel systems and sealing technologies.

As the industry moves toward higher-percentage SAF blends and eventual 100% SAF operation, aerospace manufacturers must ensure elastomeric seals remain compatible with evolving fuel chemistries while maintaining performance under demanding aerospace operating conditions. Changes in aromatic content could alter seal swelling behaviour, while prolonged fuel exposure, thermal ageing, dry-out events and fuel switching could affect long-term reliability and sealing effectiveness. Recent testing of aerospace-grade FKM compounds demonstrated stable performance across multiple SAF pathways and blend formulations, supporting their suitability for long-term aerospace applications.

Depending on feedstock and production pathway, SAF can reduce lifecycle greenhouse gas emissions by more than 65% compared with conventional jet fuel. The industry specification ASTM D7566 has established multiple approved SAF pathways, enabling fuels derived from biomass, agricultural residues, plant oils, algal oils and alcohol-based feedstocks to enter commercial aviation use. However, not all SAF pathways are chemically identical, and differences in fuel composition have the potential to significantly influence elastomer performance and long-term sealing reliability.

This issue is becoming increasingly important because SAF deployment depends heavily on preserving “drop-in” compatibility. Large-scale adoption becomes considerably more difficult if aircraft systems require extensive redesign or recertification to accommodate new fuel formulations. As a result, advanced materials validation is emerging as a critical enabler of scalable SAF implementation across both existing and future aerospace platforms.

Why fuel chemistry matters

The compatibility challenge surrounding SAF is rooted primarily in fuel chemistry. Under ASTM D7566, several approved SAF pathways exist, including FT-SPK (Fischer-Tropsch Synthetic Paraffinic Kerosene), HEFA-SPK (Hydroprocessed Esters and Fatty Acids Synthetic Paraffinic Kerosene) and ATJ-SPK (Alcohol-to-Jet Synthetic Paraffinic Kerosene). Although all qualify as sustainable aviation fuels, their chemical compositions differ from conventional Jet A fuel and from one another. One of the most significant variables is aromatic content.

Traditional jet fuels contain approximately 15% aromatic hydrocarbons that influence elastomer swelling behaviour. Controlled swell is essential because seals rely on dimensional conformity to maintain reliable sealing performance under changing thermal and operational conditions. Excessive swell can weaken materials and reduce dimensional stability, while insufficient swell can compromise sealing effectiveness. Previous studies show that Nitrile (NBR) seals exposed to jet fuel do require fuel containing aromatic content to ensure sufficient level of swell behaviour.

The challenges regarding SAF adoption become more pronounced as the aviation sector evaluates higher-percentage SAF blends and eventual 100% SAF operation. These synthetic paraffinic fuel pathways contain little or no aromatic content, potentially altering how elastomeric materials absorb fuel and behave during prolonged exposure.

As a result of this, the practical use of SAF has therefore required blending with conventional jet fuel, often at 50/50 ratios, to maintain aromatic levels compatible with existing fuel-system architectures.

To address this, the industry has also explored Synthetic Aromatic Kerosene (SAK), which introduces aromatic compounds back into sustainable fuel blends. Rather than functioning as a standalone fuel, SAK can act as a blending component capable of restoring aromatic balance while supporting fully sustainable fuel formulations.

Testing programmes have therefore examined blends containing approximately 20% SAK with 80% SAF (to achieve the target aromatic content) to evaluate the performance of seal materials exposed to these fluids.

Evaluating elastomer performance under SAF exposure

Greene Tweed's testing programme recently evaluated Fusion FKM compounds at temperatures up to 125°C across dry-out, fluid ageing, and fuel-switching scenarios, conditions designed to replicate the conditions that aircraft will encounter. The results showed consistent hardness retention and controlled volume swell across all three SPK pathways and SAK-enhanced blends.

The study examined multiple aerospace-grade fluoroelastomer compounds (including FKM Fusion 731, 772 and 665) alongside fluorosilicone FVMQ 409 materials across FT-SPK, HEFA-SPK and ATJ-SPK fuels, 50/50 SAF-control fuel blends and SAK-enhanced formulations, intended to simulate higher-SAF-content operating conditions.

The testing conditions were designed to replicate representative aerospace operating environments rather than simple laboratory immersion studies alone. Materials were subjected to prolonged fuel exposure, thermal ageing, dry-out conditions and fuel-switching scenarios at temperatures reaching 125°C.

The Fusion FKM compounds demonstrated relatively stable hardness characteristics and controlled volume swell across the evaluated SAF pathways and blend conditions. As shown in Figure 1, hardness changes following dry-out exposure remained relatively limited across the 50/50 SAF-control fuel blends, despite some limited variation between FT-SPK, HEFA-SPK and ATJ-SPK formulations. These results (combined with the other assessments that were performed) indicate that the evaluated FKM materials maintained stable performance across multiple SAF pathways under representative aerospace operating conditions. Their performance also remained comparatively stable during fluid ageing, dry-out exposure and fuel-switching evaluations.

The fluorosilicone material behaved differently. Greater variability in hardness retention and higher swell behaviour were observed under several SAF conditions, particularly during dry-out and fuel-switching evaluations where dimensional changes increased following transitions between control fuel and SAF blends.

These findings are operationally significant because aircraft may operate on conventional Jet A (or Jet A-1), blended SAF and future higher-SAF-content fuels, depending on airport infrastructure and regional fuel availability. Repeated transitions between fuel types could create fluctuating swell conditions that might affect long-term fluorosilicone seal performance. The evaluations also revealed differences between SAF pathways themselves.

HEFA-SPK blends generally produced lower volume-change behaviour in the seal materials after dry-out exposure compared with FT-SPK and ATJ-SPK blends. ATJ-SPK blends meanwhile produced slightly higher swell characteristics after dry-out in several cases. These distinctions reinforce the point that SAF cannot be treated as a chemically uniform category from a materials perspective.

The above findings were reinforced by the results of subsequent evaluations using SAK fluid blends. As shown in Figure 2, the FKM compounds maintained comparatively consistent hardness performance across the 20% SAK / 80% SAF blends, while fluorosilicone materials continued to show greater variability. These findings support the approach of aromatic balancing in preserving elastomer compatibility as SAF formulations evolve toward higher sustainable fuel content.

Beyond hardness and volume swell, broader validation work also included tensile strength, elongation, modulus and compression-set evaluations. These additional metrics are important because aerospace sealing reliability depends on maintaining long-term mechanical integrity under prolonged operational exposure.

Why materials validation can help to shape scalable SAF deployment

As SAF adoption expands, materials validation is becoming increasingly important across aerospace manufacturing and operations.

The challenge is not simply determining whether materials can tolerate short-term SAF exposure. Aerospace manufacturers and operators require confidence that sealing materials will maintain reliable performance across varying fuel blends, operational environments and long-term service conditions.

This is particularly important because SAF deployment is intended to scale without major aircraft system redesigns. The economic and operational logic behind SAF depends on maintaining compatibility with existing engines, fuel systems and fuelling infrastructure, where sealing products play a critical role in maintaining safety, reliability, and performance, while avoiding costly recertification and production disruption.

Current testing confirms the compatibility of FKM materials, such as the Greene Tweed’s Fusion portfolio, in SAF applications without requiring the modification of existing aerospace sealing architectures. Stable performance across FT-SPK, HEFA-SPK, ATJ-SPK and SAK-enhanced blends indicates that advanced fluorinated elastomers can tolerate evolving fuel compositions while maintaining sealing reliability under representative aerospace conditions. At the same time, ongoing validation remains essential.

Evaluations performed to date have been conducted using single batches of elastomer compounds and individual fuel production lots. Longer-duration exposure studies, expanded thermal ageing evaluations and additional fuel-pathway testing will therefore remain crucial as SAF chemistry continues to evolve and higher-percentage SAF adoption accelerates.

For aerospace manufacturers, the transition toward lower-emission flight is becoming both a fuel and a materials science challenge. Sustainable aviation fuel may provide a practical pathway toward decarbonisation, but scalable implementation will ultimately depend on proving that aircraft systems can maintain long-term reliability while operating under increasingly diverse fuel chemistries.

text:
Jet Zero Australia closed a Series C funding round of 30 million Australian dollars (about US$21.6 million) to advance its sustainable aviation fuel (SAF) plant in Townsville, Queensland. Airbus and Qantas took part in the announcement alongside the entry of POSCO International, from South Korea, as a new investor. Japan’s Idemitsu had already joined in the previous round.

The Australian producer also reported that it received final development approval from the Queensland government for the Townsville site, a key step for Project Ulysses, its Alcohol-to-Jet (AtJ) plant that will convert bioethanol derived from agricultural by-products into SAF and renewable diesel.

Lee Sung Su, vice president of POSCO’s industrial materials division, stressed that what convinced the Korean company was not the numbers but the vision: “Australia producing its own aviation fuel, securing its own supply and growing it together with local farmers while generating jobs in the regions. We believed in that vision and want to be part of it.”

Stephen Forshaw, Airbus’ chief representative for Australia, New Zealand and the Pacific, welcomed the closing and the work of the team led by Ed Mason and Mac Irvine. He noted that, with consultations under way on the Australian government’s policy frameworks (particularly demand incentives), SAF production is one step closer. Jet Zero thanked Airbus and Qantas for their support in completing the round.

With this transaction, total investment in Jet Zero exceeds 80 million Australian dollars (about US$57.6 million). According to reports, the company’s valuation could approach 500 million Australian dollars (around US$360 million). The round, which was managed by Barrenjoey, also allows POSCO to explore fuel and feedstock offtake opportunities.

Project Ulysses, located in the Cleveland Bay Industrial Park within the Townsville State Development Area, aims to produce up to 113 million liters of low-carbon liquid fuels per year (around 90% SAF, with the remainder renewable diesel), with production start-up estimated for 2028-2029. It will use LanzaJet’s AtJ technology to process some 183 million liters of ethanol a year, and about 1,000 jobs are expected at peak construction plus more than 100 operational positions.

The project has already received public backing from ARENA (AUD 9 million, about US$6.5 million) and the Queensland government (AUD 5 million, about US$3.6 million) for the FEED study, in addition to previous investment from Qantas, Airbus and Idemitsu.

Qantas has committed to making SAF 10% of its jet fuel consumption by 2030, equivalent to around 600 million liters. Fiona Messent, Qantas’ chief sustainability officer, said domestic SAF production supports energy security, creates jobs and helps decarbonization.

Australia is seeking to develop a sovereign SAF industry amid a global supply shortage, competition for HEFA feedstocks and oil price volatility. The sector estimates that a local industry could generate tens of thousands of jobs and billions of dollars in added value, with a strong regional impact in Queensland. The Townsville plant is designed to supply airports in the north, such as Townsville and Cairns, and to strengthen fuel security in a strategic area.

The final investment decision (FID) and the demand frameworks the federal government is consulting on still need to be completed. With planning approval in hand and fresh capital from aviation, energy and manufacturing players across Asia-Pacific, Jet Zero is positioning itself as one of Australia’s most advanced AtJ projects.

title: IðunnH2 Proposes Domestic eSAF Plant for Iceland to Reduce Jet Fuel Import Dependency
description:
IðunnH2, a privately funded and locally owned project, is proposing to build a 300 MW electrofuel plant in Iceland to produce sustainable aviation fuel from renewable resources.
Iceland currently imports all of its aviation fuel, with jet fuel accounting for approximately 4% of the total value of the country's imports in 2025, around ISK 30 billion in a single year.
When operational, the plant is expected to create approximately 70 permanent positions in operations, engineering, logistics, compliance, and administration.
The project estimates annual production of around 70,000 tonnes of synthetic aviation fuel, which it describes as equivalent to approximately one-third of the Royal Air Force's entire annual aviation fuel consumption.
From 2030, EU rules under the ReFuelEU mandate require every major European airport, including Keflavík, to blend a rising share of synthetic aviation fuel.
text:
IðunnH2, a privately funded and locally owned project, is proposing to build a 300 MW electrofuel plant in Iceland to produce sustainable aviation fuel from renewable resources. The project has engaged a stakeholder group since 2022 including the municipalities of Suðurnesjabær and Reykjanesbær, Kadeco, Icelandair, Icelandic Tank Storage, and Isavia, and holds signed memoranda of understanding with Icelandic Tank Storage, Kadeco, Suðurnesjabær, Reykjanesbær, and Icelandair.

Iceland currently imports all of its aviation fuel, with jet fuel accounting for approximately 4% of the total value of the country's imports in 2025, around ISK 30 billion in a single year. Government analysis has shown jet fuel stocks at times falling below ten days of supply, short of the international 90-day standard, with fuel arriving roughly every three weeks by ship. The proposed plant would sit in Kadeco's Green Industrial Park in Suðurnesjabær, with harbour access extending into Reykjanesbær; Suðurnes accounts for close to half of all fuel sold in Iceland. The facility would direct excess heat into the local district heating system and supply by-product oxygen to nearby businesses.

The plant would purchase newly contracted renewable electricity at full market price, with its 300 MW electrolysis load designed to be curtailed in seconds when grid demand requires, serving as a demand-side reserve for homes, hospitals, and critical infrastructure on Suðurnes. The project's long-term power contracts are intended to enable financing of approximately 100 new wind turbines across two or three sites. When operational, the plant is expected to create approximately 70 permanent positions in operations, engineering, logistics, compliance, and administration. The project estimates annual production of around 70,000 tonnes of synthetic aviation fuel, which it describes as equivalent to approximately one-third of the Royal Air Force's entire annual aviation fuel consumption. One of the project's Icelandic partners, Carbon Recycling International, is described as among the world's oldest and most commercially successful e-methanol technology providers. The project is currently privately funded but will require specialised investors and EU support for construction.

From 2030, EU rules under the ReFuelEU mandate require every major European airport, including Keflavík, to blend a rising share of synthetic aviation fuel. Iceland's EEA membership entitles eligible SAF uplifted at Icelandic airports to reimbursement of 100% of the price difference against fossil kerosene, the highest tier available in the EEA. Synthetic aviation fuel is already cleared for use in NATO military aircraft at approved blend limits, and NATO Deputy Assistant Secretary General for Innovation, Hybrid and Cyber, James Appathurai, stated in July 2024 that SAF will play a key role in the alliance's energy transition efforts while maintaining military capability and interoperability.

Nearly 98.7% of visitors to Iceland arrive through Keflavík International Airport, and tourism accounted for approximately 8.8% of GDP in 2025. The project argues that a domestic SAF supply would protect Keflavík's competitiveness as a transatlantic hub as European airports face rising SAF blending obligations from 2030.

This proposal sits at the intersection of energy security and aviation decarbonisation: a country with no domestic fossil fuel production and thin jet fuel reserves is using an EU regulatory deadline to justify building its own synthetic fuel supply rather than continuing to depend entirely on imports. The approach also ties the electrolysis load into the local grid as a curtailable demand-side reserve, which is a different economic logic from a standalone fuel plant — the wind contracts underpinning the project only pencil out if the load can also serve grid balancing.

How this segment works is shaped by the ReFuelEU mandate itself: airports across Europe, including smaller hubs like Keflavík, face a rising blending requirement from 2030 regardless of whether a domestic producer exists, and Iceland's EEA-linked reimbursement tier changes the economics of who can afford to be an early domestic supplier rather than a fuel importer.

What remains to be settled is whether the specialised investors and EU support the project says it needs materialise, and whether the signed memoranda with Icelandair, Kadeco, Isavia and the two municipalities convert into binding offtake and construction commitments ahead of the 2030 blending deadline.

text:
Holcim’s Eco2fly carbon capture project at its Villaluenga de la Sagra cement plant in Toledo, Spain, has taken a further step forward with a new agreement supporting the production of synthetic sustainable aviation fuel (e-SAF).

Developed by Holcim, Eco2fly Power and Exolum, the project is expected to capture around 700,000tpa of CO2 from the cement plant. Approximately half of the captured CO2 will be combined with renewable hydrogen to produce around 100,000tpa of e-SAF, while the remainder will be permanently stored in geological formations.

The project is designed to address process emissions inherent in cement production while establishing a value chain for the utilisation of captured CO2. New facilities will be constructed alongside the Villaluenga de la Sagra plant, with start-up scheduled for 2032.

Eco2fly has now signed a memorandum of understanding with European airline Volotea for the potential supply of e-SAF over a 10-year period from the start of commercial production. Supply is expected to begin at 6.5Ml in 2032, rising to 12-19Ml in 2033-34 and 32Ml annually from 2035.

Eco2fly Project Director, Javier Esteban, said the agreement validates the project’s e-SAF production model and provides further impetus for scaling synthetic fuel production in Spain and Europe.

By combining carbon capture, utilisation and permanent storage, Eco2fly aims to provide a route for reducing emissions from cement manufacture while supplying captured CO2 as a feedstock for the decarbonisation of aviation.

title: Cathay Pacific Partners with Google to Use AI Against Global Warming: Over 100 Flights Cut ...
description:
Cathay Pacific (0293.HK) and Google announced a partnership leveraging artificial intelligence (AI) predictive technology to help pilots avoid airspace prone to "contrail" formation.
The collaboration launched in late 2025, making Cathay Pacific Google's first commercial airline partner in the Asia-Pacific region, and the first airline globally to apply contrail avoidance technology on ultra-long-haul routes.
Lawrence Fong, Cathay Pacific's Director of Digital and IT, noted: "The aviation industry needs solutions to tackle climate change, and AI is accelerating that progress."
SAF and AI: A Dual-Track Approach Cathay Pacific emphasized that it is addressing climate challenges through a multi-pronged strategy.
Google, meanwhile, is using this partnership to extend its AI capabilities into aviation operational scenarios, deepening its market position in enterprise-grade AI solutions.
text:
The aviation industry has gained a new tool in its decarbonization arsenal. Cathay Pacific (0293.HK) and Google announced a partnership leveraging artificial intelligence (AI) predictive technology to help pilots avoid airspace prone to "contrail" formation. The first-phase trial has already been applied across more than 100 Cathay flights, with over 80 of them adopting altitude adjustments, resulting in an estimated 40% reduction in the climate warming effect attributable to contrails.

The collaboration launched in late 2025, making Cathay Pacific Google's first commercial airline partner in the Asia-Pacific region, and the first airline globally to apply contrail avoidance technology on ultra-long-haul routes.

Contrails are white trails that form when water vapor from aircraft engines condenses as planes fly through cold, humid air at high altitudes. Most contrails dissipate quickly, but under specific meteorological conditions, some persist and spread into expansive cloud layers—effectively blanketing the Earth and trapping heat in the atmosphere. Research indicates that persistent contrails may account for roughly one-third of the aviation industry's total climate impact, placing them alongside carbon dioxide emissions as a critical research priority for the sector.

Michael Yue, Managing Director of Google Hong Kong, said the collaboration aims to explore "how to deploy predictive AI in real-world operations, using existing aircraft and existing fuel to help address the climate impact of contrails."

Lawrence Fong, Cathay Pacific's Director of Digital and IT, noted: "The aviation industry needs solutions to tackle climate change, and AI is accelerating that progress."

Satellite Imagery Combined with Weather Data

Google's contrail mitigation solution integrates AI predictive models, satellite imagery detection tools, and extensive meteorological data to forecast airspace prone to contrail formation. This information is made available to flight dispatchers and pilots, who can adjust flight altitudes to avoid affected areas—similar in practice to how crews currently navigate around turbulence.

Cathay Pacific, for its part, leverages onboard Wi-Fi and its proprietary electronic flight folder to give pilots real-time access to Google's predictive data and operational information, enabling more precise flight decisions.

The first-phase trial incorporated AI predictive data into actual flight planning. Beyond validating technical feasibility, it also fostered cross-departmental collaboration between flight operations and technical teams. Preliminary analysis shows that pilots often need only minor altitude adjustments to effectively prevent contrail formation.

Hong Kong–Singapore Route Delivers Standout Results

The airspace between Hong Kong and Singapore was selected as a key study route because it frequently exhibits meteorological conditions conducive to persistent contrail formation. This single route alone accounted for more than half of the total climate impact reduction achieved across the entire trial program.

Cathay Pacific noted that scientific research on contrails in the Asia-Pacific region is relatively scarce, and this collaboration will provide valuable data for global research while deepening industry understanding of contrail formation mechanisms and mitigation measures in Asia-Pacific airspace.

Both parties are now preparing a larger second-phase trial that will span Cathay's Asian and trans-Pacific route network to gather more real-world operational data. Additionally, they are collaborating with the nonprofit Contrails.org to build a more comprehensive operational database that advances scientific research on contrail mitigation.

SAF and AI: A Dual-Track Approach

Cathay Pacific emphasized that it is addressing climate challenges through a multi-pronged strategy. On the carbon dioxide reduction front, the airline continues to modernize its fleet, enhance operational efficiency, and adopt Sustainable Aviation Fuel (SAF). At the same time, it is actively focusing on the aviation industry's non-CO₂ emissions, including scientific research into the climate impact of contrails.

The aviation industry's climate impact has long centered on carbon dioxide, but in recent years the scientific community has placed growing emphasis on non-CO₂ effects. The warming effect of contrails varies by altitude, time of day, and geographic location. Persistent contrails formed at night have a particularly pronounced warming effect because the absence of sunlight reflection fails to offset their heat-trapping properties. This makes AI-driven precision forecasting and avoidance of high-risk airspace one of the most cost-effective emissions reduction measures available in the near term.

Compared to the capital investment and supply chain development required for fleet replacement or large-scale adoption of sustainable fuels, the marginal cost of adjusting flight altitudes is extremely low—yet it can deliver quantifiable climate benefits on specific routes. If second-phase trial data continues to support the first-phase findings, this technology could become a standard practice for the aviation industry in addressing non-CO₂ climate effects.

For investors, Cathay Pacific's positioning in sustainable aviation not only responds to increasingly stringent carbon disclosure requirements from regulators but also helps mitigate potential future carbon taxes or emissions trading costs. Google, meanwhile, is using this partnership to extend its AI capabilities into aviation operational scenarios, deepening its market position in enterprise-grade AI solutions.

The 10th Riga Aviation Forum will bring together aviation leaders, policymakers and business executives from the Baltics, Nordics and Europe on 10 September 2026.

The leading aviation industry conference in the Baltic region, the Riga Aviation Forum, will bring together aviation leaders, policymakers, experts and business executives from the Baltics, the Nordics and across Europe on 10 September 2026 at Hanzas Perons in Riga. Participants will discuss the future of aviation and related industries, including their role in regional economic growth, connectivity, manufacturing and innovation.

Organized by the Latvian Aviation Association in cooperation with its partners, the Riga Aviation Forum is marking its 10th anniversary in 2026. Over the past decade, the event has developed into a meeting place for aviation decision-makers in the Baltic region and a platform for dialogue between the aviation industry, government institutions, tourism stakeholders and international organizations.

The 2026 programme will be opened by Latvia’s Minister of Transport, Rihards Kozlovskis, and will address trends and challenges shaping aviation development at regional and global level.

The Forum’s keynote discussion, moderated by Raimonds Gruntiņš, Regional Director Europe at the International Air Transport Association (IATA), will feature Sanders Salmu, Deputy Secretary General of the Estonian Ministry of Climate; Elīna Šimiņa-Neverovska, Deputy State Secretary at Latvia’s Ministry of Transport; Erno Hildén, CEO and President of Latvia’s national airline airBaltic; and Lithuanian aviation industry professional Gediminas Almantas. The discussion will focus on aviation policymaking at national, regional and European levels.

Another session will examine cooperation between government institutions, tourism organizations and aviation industry stakeholders in relation to economic growth. Participants will include Laila Odiņa, CEO of RIX Riga Airport; Ieva Jāgere, Director of the Investment and Development Agency of Latvia (LIAA); Olga Gončarova, Head of Lithuania Travel; and Mari Saloniemi, representative of Visit Tampere.

Also read → Riga Aviation Forum 2025 gathers Baltic and European leaders

Workforce development and talent attraction will also be addressed by aviation and human resources professionals, including international aviation specialist Jane Hoskisson, Iluta Savicka, Head of Norwegian’s Riga Base, and Aivars Pūcītis, Board Member of Latvijas Gaisa Satiksme.

The transition from traditional infrastructure development to integrated and intelligent aviation ecosystems at Baltic airports will be explored by experts representing SITA, as well as executives from Latvijas Gaisa Satiksme and Lithuania’s aviation industry association CAVIA.

A dedicated session will focus on businesses operating “behind the runway”, covering sectors closely linked to aviation and their role in industry growth as airports develop into new forms of urban environments. Speakers will include Walter Seib, Chairman of Avolta; Borga Dincler, Business Development and Marketing Director at Turkish airport advertising operator Media Port; and Aude Ferrand, Chairwoman of TAV Operation Services and Chief Commercial Officer of TAV Airports.

The Forum will also address manufacturing and supply chains, including their resilience and ability to adapt to sustainability challenges and rapid industry transformation. Speakers will include Jānis Kisiels, CEO of sustainable aviation fuel producer NorSAF; Gytis Leonavicius, CEO of Lithuania’s Skyco; and representatives of AM Craft, Axon Cable and Artex Latvia.

“We are particularly pleased that, in this anniversary year, the Riga Aviation Forum will gain a broader regional dimension by connecting the Baltics and the Nordics through a live discussion linking the Riga Aviation Forum with the Tampere Business Forum and Tampere Aviation Forum in Finland. During this session, Baltic and Nordic experts will discuss regional connectivity, economic cooperation, investment opportunities, and cross-border business development,” says Zigmārs Vestfāls, Head of the Latvian Aviation Association.

In addition to the conference programme, RAF 2026 will offer networking opportunities for aviation professionals, business leaders, public sector representatives, investors and representatives of international organizations from across Europe.

text:
7th September 2026 – (Hong Kong) Cathay Pacific and Google have announced their collaboration on an ambitious project to advance research into contrails and their implications for aviation’s climate footprint. This partnership marks Cathay Pacific as Google’s inaugural commercial airline partner in Asia-Pacific for AI-driven contrail mitigation technology, and notably, the first airline worldwide to explore contrail avoidance on ultra-long-haul services. The trials, already underway across Cathay Pacific’s extensive global network, seek to evaluate both the practical viability and operational limitations associated with mitigating contrails generated by aircraft.

Contrails, or condensation trails, appear as thin white lines behind aircraft and are formed when aeroplanes pass through cold, humid conditions at high altitude. While some contrails dissipate quickly, others persist and spread, resulting in larger cloud formations which can trap heat within the earth’s atmosphere. Scientific studies indicate that these long-lasting contrails could account for approximately one-third of aviation’s total climate impact, underscoring the importance of understanding and reducing their occurrence in addition to tackling carbon dioxide emissions.

Cathay Pacific has long recognised the airline industry’s environmental responsibilities, with an ongoing focus on minimising carbon dioxide emissions through fleet modernisation, operational enhancements, and the adoption of sustainable aviation fuel. However, the airline also acknowledges the significance of non-carbon climate effects, such as those produced by contrails. Working with Google, Cathay Pacific is supplying valuable operational data through flight trials, furthering global research into contrail formation and avoidance. These efforts are expected to yield new insights regarding the potential climate benefits of contrail mitigation across real-world flight conditions, particularly in regions such as Asia-Pacific which have been underrepresented in previous studies.

Google’s solution integrates artificial intelligence-based predictive models, satellite imagery, and sophisticated weather analysis to anticipate when and where contrails are most likely to form. This data enables both flight dispatchers and pilots to make considered altitude adjustments, similar to standard procedures for evading turbulence. Cathay Pacific’s pilots, utilising the company’s modern fleet with advanced connectivity and its proprietary Electronic Flight Folder system, can access live Google contrail forecasts alongside key operational information, promoting timely and seamless decision-making in the cockpit.

Since late 2025, the ongoing operational trial has targeted more than one hundred flights across Cathay Pacific’s network. Over eighty of these journeys were routed to avoid predicted contrail zones, with Google estimating that these efforts have resulted in approximately a forty per cent reduction in the warming effect caused by contrails.

title: Frontex-supported returns climb in first half of 2026 - European Union
description:
In the first half of the year, 109 Return Specialists were working across 15 Member States.
Around 14 000 people registered for EU reintegration assistance in the first half of 2026, up from around 8 000 a year earlier.
Member States may also enrol other returnees for the EURP as long as they meet the eligibility criteria.
The Commission is expected to propose a further strengthening of Frontex’s mandate on returns, including its support to Member States, in the autumn.
Established in 2004, the Agency’s tasks include monitoring migratory flows, supporting border management, and assisting Member States with return activities.
text:
Frontex, the European Border and Coast Guard Agency, helped EU Member States return more than 33 000 people to non-EU countries in the first half of 2026, up from around 30 000 in the same period a year earlier. Around two in three of them returned voluntarily.

Some 21 000 people returned voluntarily in the first half of the year, compared with around 19 000 a year earlier. Every return that Frontex supports follows an enforceable return decision, meaning the person has exhausted their legal options to remain in the EU. In a voluntary return, the person complies with that decision and leaves with practical help and, where they qualify, financial support. In a forced return, the decision is enforced because the person has not complied with the obligation to leave. That obligation is the same in both cases.

Whether a return is voluntary or forced is decided by national authorities rather than by Frontex; however, the Agency supports both. Voluntary returns are generally more cost-effective than forced ones, which routinely require escorts, medical and monitoring staff, and in some cases dedicated charter arrangements.

Return Specialists from the Standing Corps talk to people about what returning would involve and what help is available, help national authorities manage cases in the systems used to process returns, and support obtaining from the authorities of countries of origin the identity documents required to travel. In the first half of the year, 109 Return Specialists were working across 15 Member States.

The support does not always stop when the plane lands. Around 14 000 people registered for EU reintegration assistance in the first half of 2026, up from around 8 000 a year earlier. That assistance can mean vocational training, a small grant to start a business, or counselling once someone is back in their country of origin. More than four in five of those who registered had returned voluntarily.*

*Not all the people registered under the EU Reintegration Programme (EURP) were the same people as those returned with Frontex support. Member States may also enrol other returnees for the EURP as long as they meet the eligibility criteria.

The Agency also operationally supports the departures themselves. Frontex Return Escort and Support Officers (FRESOs), also part of the Standing Corps, accompany returnees, help people through airports, and handle the administrative and logistical work behind each flight, including for voluntary returnees who need extra assistance. Over the period, 118 FRESOs were deployed across 11 Member States.

The wider legal framework for returns is also changing. The Regulation establishing a Common European System for Returns, agreed by the European Parliament and the Council in June 2026, sets out common rules for return across the EU, including by making forced return the rule where a person does not cooperate, absconds to another Member State, or poses a security risk. The Commission is expected to propose a further strengthening of Frontex’s mandate on returns, including its support to Member States, in the autumn.

A lower-carbon approach to return flights

With air travel accounting for the large majority of return operations, Frontex has been working to reduce the environmental footprint of its return flights. The Agency prioritises scheduled flights over charter flights whenever this is operationally possible. Under an agreement in place since 2023 with a major European airline, a share of the airline’s revenue from Frontex-funded flights goes towards purchasing Sustainable Aviation Fuel (SAF) and other environmental sustainability initiatives, provided that they meet the sustainability criteria set by the International Civil Aviation Organization. In the first half of 2026, this funded the purchase of over 90 tonnes of SAF, mitigating an estimated 313 tonnes of CO2 across the full lifecycle of the fuel, from production to combustion.

Frontex, the European Border and Coast Guard Agency, supports EU Member States and Schengen-associated Countries in managing the external borders of the European Union. Established in 2004, the Agency’s tasks include monitoring migratory flows, supporting border management, and assisting Member States with return activities. Frontex is building up a Standing Corps of officers who can be deployed to support national authorities on the ground. The Agency is based in Warsaw, Poland.

IAR’s Airport Leader of the Year 2026 will be announced at the Airport Honour Awards taking place during the International Airport Summit in Rome on 11 November.
text:
If you missed part 1 of the interview, you can read it here.

When Christina Cassotis arrived at Pittsburgh International Airport (PIT) in 2015, many still viewed it through the lens of the hub that it had lost. A decade later, the airport has pioneered everything from on-site childcare facilities to microgrids to sustainable aviation fuel production and a terminal built for all travellers.

Christina opened the landmark $1.7 billion new terminal on 18 November 2025, the result of more than a decade of planning and four years of construction. The new terminal is viewed by the industry as setting new benchmarks in sustainability, experience and innovation. International Airport Review Editor, Holly Miles, recently met with the airport CEO to discuss the vision for the terminal and what this means for passengers.

An airport built for the local community

Christina said on opening the terminal that it was a “an airport built for Pittsburgh, by Pittsburgh.”

With air travel demand set to double by 2050, the number of travellers with special requirements will increase at Pittsburgh and other airports around the world.

According to Cassotis, the new terminal is designed with accessibility “from the very beginning, from the ground-up” because their mantra is that everyone deserves the right to travel, and they strive to be one of the most accessible airports in the world. It was this goal that saw the airport receive Universal Design Certification from the University at Buffalo’s Centre for Inclusive Design and Environmental Access (IDEA Centre) – the only airport to be awarded this so far.

“We all have an obligation to make physical infrastructure as accessible as possible. We built that into the project from day one, working with groups from across the region and specialists in sustainability, technology, accessibility and other areas.”

In each of the four concourses there are restrooms with universal changing tables, increased seating and rest options, raised crosswalks, accessible height ticketing counters, and improved wayfinding to create a more accessible experience.

The airport also runs a “We Got You” initiative, which is a cross-functional programme designed to assist travellers using people, technology and process. Volunteer ambassadors and customer service staff are equipped with hand-held devices to help passengers more quickly.

For passengers with autism or sensory sensitivities, Presley’s Place is a sensory room located in Concourse A, where they can escape the noisy airport environment and relax.

For mothers, the airport also features two nursing rooms stocked with healthy snacks, bottled water, and words of encouragement from fellow parents written on Post-it notes that adorn the walls as a personal touch.

Recognising that childcare can be a barrier to potential airport employees taking up work and a factor in employees leaving the company, Cassotis took a revolutionary step and opened an on-site childcare facility in September 2023. Providing a childcare option on the same site as an employee’s workplace helps strengthen parents’ work-life balance and supports workforce development – and PIT remains one of the few airports in the world that offer this benefit.

Pittsburgh is one of 325 airports that partner with the Hidden Disabilities Sunflower programme. A discreet lanyard, bracelet, pin or sticker lets airport team members know that the wearer has a hidden disability and may require additional help.

If you are a dog lover, you may be lucky enough to see one of the PIT PAWS – short for pups alleviating worry and stress – the therapy dogs who roam the airport with their ambassador to bring joy (as well as helpful information and tips from the handler) to passengers before their flights.

A duty to resilience

For Christina’s community, which operates as a major transplant centre, people’s lives literally depend on the airport. “People’s lives depend on transplant teams getting in or organs being delivered. If we shut down for a day, it could literally cost somebody their life. I feel that’s a responsibility we all have in this industry: to operate with as much resilience and redundancy as possible.”

This means creating an incredibly resilient airport, which they are doing by linking with manufacturing start-ups, energy developments and tech innovation to ensure that they are fit for multiple different futures and what challenges that would bring.

“We’ve prepared for technologies that we can’t even imagine yet. We made sure fibre runs throughout the terminal, and we’ve ensured that we can expand if required. If a hub operation ever returned, we’re master-planned to add more gates. We also have land available if we need to expand parking or other facilities.”

Having seen other airports such as Los Angeles, Atlanta and Heathrow make headlines due to major power outages, Cassotis decided that this could not happen to them. So, in July 2021, PIT became the first major airport in the world to be entirely powered by on-site natural gas and solar energy through a 23MW microgrid.

“We sit on a large site with access to natural gas, so we developed a microgrid through private sector partners at no cost to the airport. The system produces 23MW of energy while we use around 15MW. Excess power is sold back to the grid. The grid is now our backup rather than our primary power source.”

When the same thing happened to their airport, and fires damaged two of PIT’s substations in March 2025, the microgrid isolated those interconnections, powered the airport independently and prevented any loss of power.

“We’ve saved more than $1 million in utility costs annually, reduced our carbon footprint and created a highly resilient energy system, supported by five natural gas turbines and 10,000 solar panels.”

SAF to take off at PIT

Pittsburgh aims to become the first U.S. airport to produce sustainable aviation fuel on-site and this is something Cassotis believes will drive economic development for both the region and the airport, while helping the airport meet its decarbonisation goals.

“Space and resources prevent some airports from pursuing similar projects, but we hope others will follow. We’re progressing towards development and securing offtake agreements. The project will improve resilience for airlines, while increasing domestic energy production. Our airlines are very supportive of this.”

The airport has pipeline access to the river, which would grant them the opportunity to export fuel by barge or rail, allowing them to supply airports across the U.S. Northeast and Midwest.

The Allegheny County Airport Authority also has ambitions to produce hydrogen on-site which would revolutionise the aviation industry. On-site hydrogen would also be used to power ground vehicles, facilities and fuel cells if realised.

Cassotis is a visionary leader who clearly has her eyes on the future and is laying the groundwork to ensure the airport delivers a fantastic passenger experience and plays a leading role in its community and global aviation for many years to come.

Unfortunately, because Christina was opening her new terminal, she was not able to attend the awards ceremony to be presented with her International Airport Review Airport Leader of the Year Award, but this only serves to further highlight her dedication to her airport and her staff. Cassotis sent in the acceptance video below, which was played at the 2025 event.

IAR’s Airport Leader of the Year 2026 will be announced at the Airport Honour Awards taking place during the International Airport Summit in Rome on 11 November.

text:
Amid sweeping changes in global energy markets, GS Caltex Vice Chair Hur Sae-hong seeks to move South Korea’s energy and chemical company beyond its decades-old focus on refining volumes toward higher-value, lower-carbon businesses.

Hur outlined his vision in McKinsey & Co.’s “Leading Asia” interview series and its centennial book, “Shapers & Founders: The Untold Stories of Asia’s Extraordinary Owner-CEOs.” He was featured alongside other Korean business leaders from companies including HD Hyundai and MBK Partners.

A fourth-generation member of GS Group’s founding family, Hur spent more than 18 years working in Japan, the US and Singapore for companies including IBM and Chevron. Those experiences helped shape a management philosophy that combines global adaptability with what he describes as traditional Korean humility.

At its center is “we-dership,” Hur’s term for leadership built collectively. The idea calls on executives to “lead from the top, but move together,” with teamwork underpinning the company’s ambition to remain competitive for the next century.

GS Caltex, Korea’s first private oil refiner, operates the world’s fourth-largest single-site refinery. The company prospered for decades on surging energy demand across Asia, but slowing global growth and the risk of excess supply have challenged its traditional volume-led model.

“How can we maintain a growth path on a quality basis to ensure we remain sustainable for the future?” Hur said.

His answer is what GS Caltex calls its “Deep Transformation Journey,” built around three pillars of transformation: business, digital and artificial intelligence, and green transformation.

Business transformation, which the company calls BX, seeks to overhaul its mindset, culture and organizational structure. Digital and AI transformation, or DAX, focuses on building capabilities internally, including retraining and refining petrochemical engineers through an in-house digital academy.

Green transformation, or GX, seeks to shift the company’s portfolio toward lower-carbon growth areas. These include sustainable aviation fuel, bio-based marine fuel, circular plastics, clean hydrogen, and carbon capture, utilization and storage.

Hur is also pushing for GS Caltex to build what he calls a “black-box advantage” — an internal combination of work processes, organizational capabilities and corporate culture that competitors would struggle to replicate.

Investing in emerging green businesses carries substantial risk, but Hur argues that standing still poses an even greater threat. He describes the status quo as “a killer of sustainable growth.”

To manage that risk, GS Caltex uses marginal abatement cost curves to assess projects according to their cost and emissions-reduction potential, prioritizing lower-risk opportunities.

Hur is also trying to preserve startuplike agility within a large corporation. A newly created "business council" brings senior executives together to lead cross-company strategic projects that might otherwise remain confined within individual business units.

Named one of Stanford Graduate School of Business’ “Centennial Alumni Catalysts” in 2025, Hur said the success of the strategy would ultimately be judged by measurable results.

“For me, sustainability means fundamentally rebalancing our portfolio toward lower-carbon businesses,” he said. “In the end, I believe the only way to demonstrate this commitment is through outcomes, not words.”

title: Innovative Machine Learning Models Advance Soil and Plant Water Tracking
description:
Water typically moves from the land to the atmosphere through soil evaporation and plant transpiration.
However, many existing computer models struggle to distinguish between soil evaporation and plant transpiration.
Researchers developed a hybrid model that provides data-informed estimates of parameters that are difficult to estimate.
Summary Accurately representing evapotranspiration and its partitioning between soil evaporation and plant transpiration is a long-standing challenge in Earth system science.
A multi-institutional team of researchers developed a hybrid evapotranspiration model that integrates machine learning into the Penman–Monteith modeling framework to estimate key surface conductance values while preserving physical constraints.
text:
Water typically moves from the land to the atmosphere through soil evaporation and plant transpiration. This process is called evapotranspiration. It plays a major role in events such as drought and heat waves. However, many existing computer models struggle to distinguish between soil evaporation and plant transpiration.

Researchers developed a hybrid model that provides data-informed estimates of parameters that are difficult to estimate. The model combines a physical framework with machine learning to improve predictions of evapotranspiration and its components across diverse conditions, including heat waves and drought.

The Impact

Understanding and predicting how ecosystems use water is essential to helping communities prepare for heat waves and droughts. A new hybrid model combines a form of artificial intelligence and insights from existing land surface models to create a hybrid model that improves scientists' understanding of Earth system processes. This hybrid approach reveals how environmental factors influence evaporation and transpiration across ecosystems. These factors include radiation, soil moisture, and vegetation. These insights can help scientists improve land surface models in Earth system simulations while highlighting where traditional representations of processes break down and where methods that are physically constrained and data-informed may improve robustness.

Summary

Accurately representing evapotranspiration and its partitioning between soil evaporation and plant transpiration is a long-standing challenge in Earth system science. A multi-institutional team of researchers developed a hybrid evapotranspiration model that integrates machine learning into the Penman–Monteith modeling framework to estimate key surface conductance values while preserving physical constraints. Researchers evaluated the model using observations from 47 National Ecological Observatory Network sites spanning a wide range of environment and vegetation types. The model consistently outperformed traditional physics-based models and purely machine learning approaches, maintained accuracy at new sites, and remained stable under extreme conditions. These results demonstrate a scalable, physically grounded pathway for improving understanding of ecosystem water fluxes.

Funding

This work was primarily supported by the Environmental System Science program within the U.S. Department of Energy Office of Science's Biological and Environmental Research program. Support was also received from the Zegar Family Foundation and the National Science Foundation Division of Environmental Biology.

text:
Once completed, the CIF will be Europe’s largest laboratory infrastructure specifically designed for science-based technology transfer and pre-startup teams in green chemistry. Here, researchers will be able to further develop their findings under real-world conditions, validate them for specific applications, and prepare to launch their startups.

From a construction standpoint, the CIF also marks an important milestone for TU Berlin: Following the TEM electron microscopy building, it is the second new building in many years that the university is constructing as the project owner. Approximately 20 million euros have been allocated for the project. Seven million euros of this amount come from the State of Berlin’s Special Fund for Infrastructure of the Growing City and Sustainability (SIWANA), while TU Berlin is contributing approximately 13 million euros. Construction work is on schedule and within budget, with completion planned for 2027.

Biotech start-up scales green chemistry with new investment
